title: Retrospective analysis of parallel platelet count determinations in EDTA and citrate blood for exclusion of pseudothrombocytopenia
summary:
Pseudothrombocytopenia (PTCP) does not represent an actual decrease in platelet count within the patient’s circulation. Instead, it represents a laboratory artifact that results in spuriously low platelet counts. One of the most common causes of PTCP is the clumping of platelets in tubes containing the anticoagulant EDTA. An anticoagulant is regularly used to prevent blood clotting in blood collection tubes. Electronic cell counters cannot recognize these platelet clumps as individual cells, and therefore the platelet count is measured as spuriously low. Patients with PTCP do not have an increased risk of bleeding events. Nevertheless, accurate measurement of the platelet count is essential to prevent unnecessary diagnostic or therapeutic interventions. To identify PTCP, an alternative anticoagulant such as citrate may be used, or a microscopic examination for platelet clumps may be performed.

The aim of this study is to retrospectively analyze the results of parallel measurements of platelet counts in EDTA- and citrate-anticoagulated blood samples since 2014. Furthermore, clinical conditions and laboratory findings associated with an increased likelihood of pseudothrombocytopenia occurrence should be identified.  
The study retrospectively evaluates data from patients of Frankfurt University Hospital who underwent parallel platelet measurement in EDTA and citrate blood during the period between 01/2014 and 05/2026. A number of approximately n=1000 patients is planned.
Primarily the total number of measurements performed and the percentage of confirmed pseudothrombocytopenia will be determined. If a microscopic blood smear was performed to evaluate platelet clumps, its findings will also be included in the analysis. In cases where the platelet count in citrate blood is higher than in EDTA blood, additional clinical information will be collected. This includes data regarding the clinical context of measurement, underlying disease, bleeding history, medication and comorbidities.
